prompt: Felipe Arruda runs Mantiqueira's ERP. Which product line does it descend from?
hint: The table of names in the section.

choices.text: Axapta, through Dynamics AX
choices.why: That line became Finance and Supply Chain Management, the ERP built for large companies.

choices.text: Dynamics CRM
choices.why: Dynamics CRM became the sales and service apps on Dataverse; it was never an ERP.

choices.text: Navision, through Dynamics NAV
choices.why: Right: Business Central is NAV renamed and rebuilt, and NAV was Navision's product before Microsoft bought the company in 2002.

choices.text: Great Plains, Microsoft's first accounting acquisition
choices.why: Great Plains was bought in 2001 and is a separate line; Business Central does not come from it.

prompt: Microsoft announces an update to Business Central's base application. What does Felipe have to do with Mantiqueira's six extensions?
hint: What an extension is not allowed to touch.

choices.text: Merge their changes into the new base code, as NAV partners did with C/AL
choices.why: That was the NAV model, where partners edited the base. Business Central online does not let anybody modify the base, so there is nothing to merge.

choices.text: Test them against the new version in a sandbox
choices.why: Right: the extensions sit beside the base and attach to published events, so they survive the update; Felipe's job is to check that they still behave.

choices.text: Ask the partner to rewrite them in X++ for the new release
choices.why: X++ is the language of Finance and Supply Chain Management. Business Central extensions are written in AL and are not rewritten per release.

choices.text: Delay the update until the extensions are certified
choices.why: In the online version Microsoft updates the base on its own schedule. The protection is that extensions never changed the base, not that the customer holds the update back.

prompt: Marketing builds a Power App on Dataverse and wants Mantiqueira's customers in it. Regina says it should be easy, since both are Dynamics. What is actually true?
hint: Where Business Central keeps its rows.

choices.text: The customers are already in Dataverse, because Business Central stores its data there
choices.why: Business Central keeps its own database. Dataverse is under the CRM apps and Power Apps, not under the ERPs.

choices.text: They share a sign-in, so the app can read the customers through Entra ID
choices.why: Entra ID decides who may sign in. It carries no customer records, so a shared sign-in moves no data at all.

choices.text: Nothing can connect them, since one is an ERP and the other a CRM platform
choices.why: They can be connected: Business Central has an API and can be linked to Dataverse. It is possible, not automatic.

choices.text: Something has to copy them, and that copy is an integration somebody owns
choices.why: Right: same brand is not same data. A Business Central customer is a row in Business Central until something copies it, with the delay and mapping of any copy.

prompt: The board asks whether Serra Alta should leave SAP when ECC maintenance ends. Which Microsoft ERP would be the candidate to compare, and why?
hint: What each ERP was built for, and the size of Serra Alta.

choices.text: Finance and Supply Chain Management: it is the line built for a company of Serra Alta's size
choices.why: Right: four plants, 3,200 employees, many processes and SAP's scale. That is the territory AX and its successors compete in.

choices.text: Business Central, because Mantiqueira already runs it and the group would have one ERP
choices.why: It removes the second ERP, but Business Central is built for small and mid-sized companies; sizing the group's ERP from the subsidiary is backwards.

choices.text: Dynamics 365 Sales, which would replace Salesforce at the same time
choices.why: Sales is the CRM line. It would not run finance, purchasing or production, which is what leaving SAP means.

choices.text: Dataverse, with the processes rebuilt as Power Apps
choices.why: Dataverse is a database with an API, and Power Apps builds small applications on it. Neither is an ERP for a company of this size.

prompt: A sales rep leaves and IT disables her Entra ID account. Salesforce signs in through Entra ID by SAML, with no provisioning set up. What is left in Salesforce?
hint: Single sign-on and provisioning are two halves.

choices.text: No user: disabling the account in the directory deletes it there too
choices.why: That would need provisioning, which Serra Alta never set up. SAML only governs the sign-in.

choices.text: Her user and licence, both still active
choices.why: Right: single sign-on removes a password, not an account. The user record, the licence and an API token issued earlier stay until somebody deactivates them.

choices.text: Her user, which she can still reach with her old Entra ID password
choices.why: The password lives in Entra ID, and that account is disabled. New sign-ins are blocked; it is the rest that stays.

choices.text: Only her reports, which Salesforce moves to her manager
choices.why: Nothing moves on its own. Reassigning records is somebody's manual job, which is exactly the gap.

prompt: Somebody leaves Serra Alta and IT disables their Entra ID account. In which of these systems does that, on its own, change nothing? Choose all that apply.
hint: The right-hand column of the table.

choices.text: SAP ECC
choices.why: Yes: SAP keeps its own users and passwords, so it needs a ticket of its own.

choices.text: Teams
choices.why: Teams signs in through Entra ID; the disabled account cannot open it.

choices.text: Business Central
choices.why: Yes: it signs in through Mantiqueira's old tenant, so the account Serra Alta disables is not the one it uses.

choices.text: Rota
choices.why: Rota signs in by OpenID Connect through Entra ID, so new sign-ins stop at once.

choices.text: Coleta
choices.why: Yes: an IBM i user profile, outside the directory altogether.

prompt: A lab technician at Barbacena cannot open the quality team's SharePoint site, which grants access through a dynamic group on the department field. Where is the defect?
hint: Who fills in the field the rule reads.

choices.text: In SharePoint, whose permissions should list people rather than groups
choices.why: Listing people by hand would fix one technician and break at the next hire. The group works; what it reads is wrong.

choices.text: In the dynamic group, which has not recalculated its membership yet
choices.why: The rule recalculates when attributes change, and here the attribute was wrong from the day she was hired.

choices.text: In HR's records, where a cost centre was typed into her profile
choices.why: Right: once a group grants access, the data deciding membership is security data, and the clerk filling in the hiring form was making access decisions without knowing it.

choices.text: In her licence, which does not include SharePoint
choices.why: A missing licence would stop her opening every site, not this one. Her other sites open.

prompt: Cláudia wants to stop superseded procedures being printed from Teams. Which proposal fits the lesson?
hint: Where the approved version lives.

choices.text: Move every procedure into SharePoint, where the plants already work
choices.why: It moves the copies without the approval workflow, so the uncontrolled version simply has a new home.

choices.text: Name one system of record per document type; others link to it
choices.why: Right: one system is the record for each kind of document, and the other links instead of holding a copy that drifts.

choices.text: Block file uploads in the plants' Teams channels
choices.why: The plants would keep copies on desktops and USB sticks instead. The reason they copy, Documentum being six clicks away, is untouched.

choices.text: Ask each plant to re-copy the approved version into Teams every month
choices.why: A monthly refresh still leaves a window in which the copy is out of date, and nothing tells anyone it is.

prompt: A DLP policy sorts connectors into three groups. A flow may use connectors from the Business group or from the ___ group, but not from both.
hint: The third group is Blocked.

prompt: Joana's first draft blocked the SAP connector for every flow. Why did she withdraw it?
hint: Regina's one question.

choices.text: Because a DLP policy cannot block a premium connector
choices.why: A connector can be placed in the Blocked group. The policy would have worked, which was the problem.

choices.text: Because the ESB had no capacity left for 38 more flows
choices.why: Capacity was never measured. The objection came before any question about where the flows would go.

choices.text: It broke work nobody had understood yet
choices.why: Right: blocking what people built breaks work you have not understood yet, and they would rebuild it somewhere with no inventory at all.

choices.text: Because citizen developers are entitled to build what they need
choices.why: They are, and the lesson says so, but entitlement was not the argument. The tier for writing flows still takes control away from the author.

prompt: All 38 flows reach SAP as the single user PA_FINANCEIRO. A credit limit changed in May. What does that arrangement cost Serra Alta when it asks who changed it?
hint: What SAP records about each change.

choices.text: Who acted: SAP names one user, not which flow or whose call
choices.why: Right: a shared service account turns an audit trail into a list of things that happened.

choices.text: Little, because Power Automate keeps each flow's run history
choices.why: Run history lives with each flow and expires; SAP's own record, the one an auditor reads, still names PA_FINANCEIRO for all of them.

choices.text: Speed: one user makes every flow queue behind the others
choices.why: Sharing a user does not serialise calls. The loss is knowing who acted, not throughput.

choices.text: The change itself, which SAP rejects from a service account
choices.why: SAP accepted every change; that is why the limits moved. The record of who decided is what is missing.

prompt: The planning team at Lavras built a flow that writes revised production dates into SAP every hour. Its author is the only owner. Under Joana's tiers, what should happen to it?
hint: The first condition of the last row.

choices.text: Leave it, as long as its connectors sit in the Business group
choices.why: The DLP grouping is satisfied, but DLP says nothing about who owns it or who hears when it fails.

choices.text: Add a co-owner from the planning team and leave it where it is
choices.why: That is the team tier. A flow that writes into the ERP is in the tier above.

choices.text: Switch it off and ask the planners to type the dates into SAP
choices.why: That is the block again by another name, and it trades a working flow for manual re-keying.

choices.text: Move it to a managed environment with an owning team, its own identity and alerts
choices.why: Right: a flow that writes into the ERP is an integration whoever built it, and gets what every integration gets, or is rebuilt as an official one.

prompt: Joana's first draft moved Mantiqueira into Serra Alta's SAP. What was Edson Prado's objection?
hint: Into which SAP?

choices.text: Business Central cannot export its customers and stock
choices.why: Business Central has a REST API with standard endpoints; reading its data is the easy part of any option.

choices.text: One ERP for the group is the wrong end state
choices.why: Edson did not dispute the shape. One ERP for the group is reasonable; the timing was the problem.

choices.text: ECC leaves maintenance in 2027: two migrations
choices.why: Right: once into ECC and again into S/4HANA a few years later, with the cheese extensions rebuilt in between.

choices.text: The 41 Mantiqueira users would need SAP training first
choices.why: Training is a cost of option A, but it is not what makes A the wrong choice now.

prompt: Put one month of option C, the finance-level consolidation, in order.
hint: Nothing can be read before it is closed.
items: Mantiqueira closes its month in Business Central
An integration reads the trial balance through the Business Central API
Each account is mapped onto the group chart through the controllers' table
The intercompany balances are matched and eliminated

prompt: Why does loading the intercompany NF-e XML pay off whichever of the three options is chosen?
hint: Who produced that document, and who receives it.

choices.text: Because it replaces the Business Central API for the monthly consolidation
choices.why: The XML describes individual sales. A trial balance still has to be read for consolidation.

choices.text: The sale arrives structured and authorised
choices.why: Right: the seller sends the buyer the XML SEFAZ authorised, and loading it removes the re-keying under A, B and C alike.

choices.text: Because SEFAZ requires buyers to load it into their ERP
choices.why: The lesson claims no such obligation. The argument is cost and accuracy, not compliance.

choices.text: Because it couples the two ERPs' document flows in a safe way
choices.why: It couples nothing: neither ERP calls the other. That independence is why it fits every option.

prompt: The consolidation integration will authenticate as an application registered in Mantiqueira's old tenant. What did Joana add to her plan because of that?
hint: The loose end from the previous section.

choices.text: Leave it: an application identity needs no leaver process, so the old tenant is fine
choices.why: The application has a secret that expires and is held by one person, in a tenant nobody governs. That is the loose end.

choices.text: Move Business Central into Serra Alta's tenant before the integration is built
choices.why: That move is a project with its own downtime and is not scheduled; waiting for it would delay the close by months.

choices.text: The secret goes into Rui's team's vault with its expiry dated, and the tenant move onto the S/4HANA list
choices.why: Right: the identity is registered where the ERP is, but its secret and the eventual move each get an owner.

choices.text: Authenticate with Felipe's own account, so a person is accountable for each call
choices.why: A scheduled integration should not sign in as a person; it would stop the day Felipe leaves, which is the flow problem again.

prompt: Match each earlier name to the product it is sold or known as today.
hint: Five renames from this lesson, across all four sections.

prompt: Talita proposes a Power Automate flow that creates each new key account from Salesforce as a customer in SAP. Both connectors are in the Business group. What does Joana answer?
hint: Tiers, not DLP, decide this one.

choices.text: Go ahead: the DLP policy allows it, so it is governed
choices.why: DLP only stops mixing Business and Non-business data. It says nothing about owners, monitoring or what writing into the ERP means.

choices.text: It writes into the ERP: an integration, with an owning team
choices.why: Right: the business-critical tier, whoever builds it. It may still be a flow, but not one that lives with one person in the default environment.

choices.text: Refuse it: Salesforce data may only reach SAP through Rui's ESB
choices.why: That is Joana's withdrawn first draft. The tiers allow a managed flow; what they refuse is an unowned one.

choices.text: Allow it in the team tier, with Talita and a colleague as co-owners
choices.why: A co-owner is right for a flow a team relies on. A flow that creates ERP customers is a tier higher.

prompt: Option C leaves Mantiqueira on Business Central with Felipe as its only IT person. Which part of the recommendation answers that risk?
hint: A system that one person understands.

choices.text: Moving Business Central into Serra Alta's tenant
choices.why: That closes the second identity for 41 users. It does not give Business Central a second person who knows it.

choices.text: Loading the NF-e XML instead of re-keying
choices.why: That removes two days of a clerk's month; it does nothing for the ERP if Felipe is away.

choices.text: Deciding again inside the S/4HANA project
choices.why: That fixes when the question returns, not who supports the system until then.

choices.text: A support contract with a partner, behind him
choices.why: Right: a system with one person who understands it has one point of failure, and the contract is the second person.

prompt: Across this lesson, three things nobody designed turned out to be integrations: the leaver process, Priscila's flow and the Power BI refresh. What did each lack that an official integration has?
hint: What failed silently in each story.

choices.text: A modern protocol: each used something older than REST
choices.why: Priscila's flow uses a current connector and the refresh uses the gateway. Nothing in these stories failed for the protocol.

choices.text: A licence: each ran on a free tier of Microsoft 365
choices.why: Licensing was never the failure. The refresh failed for eleven days and the leaver tickets arrived late on fully licensed systems.

choices.text: An owner who hears when it fails: each failed or could fail with nobody told
choices.why: Right: the missed SAP accounts, the unmonitored flow and the refresh failures mailed to a person who had moved on are the same gap.

choices.text: A place on the ESB, which would have retried them
choices.why: Retries would not have closed a leaver's SAP account or told anyone the dashboard was stale. The lesson moved flows to monitored homes, not all onto the ESB.
